\title{Viscosity and Intermolecular Forces}
\summary{Build a falling-ball viscometer from a ballpoint pen ball and a graduated cylinder, compare four liquids, and determine the activation energy of viscous flow for glycerin from its viscosity at five temperatures.}
\tags{viscosity, intermolecular forces, Arrhenius, Stokes' law, glycerin}
\minutes{110}

Viscosity is the part of a fluid's resistance to flow that comes from intermolecular attractions. Because a molecule must pull away from its neighbors to flow, the way viscosity falls with temperature reveals how strong those attractions are. In this lab you build a viscometer from a ballpoint pen ball and a graduated cylinder, compare four liquids, and measure glycerin at five temperatures to find the strength of the attractions between its molecules.

\info[label="For the curious: viscous and inertial drag"]{
A fluid resists a moving object in two ways. **Viscous drag** comes from layers of fluid shearing past one another near the object's surface; it is proportional to the object's speed and to the viscosity, and it is what Stokes' law describes. **Inertial drag** comes from the object having to push fluid out of its way and leave a wake behind it; it is proportional to the fluid's density and to the square of the speed, and it does not depend on viscosity at all. Which one dominates is set by the Reynolds number, $\mathrm{Re} = \rho v d / \eta$, the ratio of inertial to viscous forces. A 1 mm ball creeping through glycerin or corn syrup has $\mathrm{Re}$ well below 1, so viscous drag is essentially the whole story and the fall time measures viscosity. The same ball in water has $\mathrm{Re}$ in the hundreds: inertial drag dominates, the fall time says almost nothing about viscosity, and Stokes' law does not apply.
}

# Equations

Stokes' law for a small sphere falling at terminal velocity $v$:

$$\eta = \frac{2 r^2 (\rho_\mathrm{ball} - \rho_\mathrm{liquid})\, g}{9 v}$$

where $\eta$ is the viscosity ($\pu{Pa s}$), $r$ the ball radius (m), $\rho_\mathrm{ball}$ and $\rho_\mathrm{liquid}$ the densities ($\pu{kg/m^3}$), $g = \pu{9.81 m/s^2}$, and $v$ the terminal velocity (m/s).

Arrhenius equation for viscosity:

$$\eta = \eta_0 \, e^{E_a / RT} \qquad \text{so} \qquad \ln \eta = \ln \eta_0 + \frac{E_a}{R}\cdot\frac{1}{T}$$

where $E_a$ is the activation energy of viscous flow (J/mol), $R = \pu{8.314 J mol^-1 K^-1}$, $T$ the absolute temperature (K), and $\eta_0$ a constant. A plot of $\ln \eta$ against $1/T$ is a straight line of slope $E_a/R$.

# Materials

**Chemicals**

- [ ] Glycerin (glycerol), 99% or higher, from a pharmacy: one bottle of at least 120 mL. Vegetable glycerin sold for skin care is the same product.
- [ ] Light corn syrup, about 100 mL
- [ ] Dish soap, about 100 mL
- [ ] Tap water

**Equipment**

- [ ] BIC Cristal or Round Stic medium ballpoint pen (one)
- [ ] Small strong magnet (a neodymium magnet, or a refrigerator magnet)
- [ ] 100 mL graduated cylinder
- [ ] Wire cutter, diagonal cutter, flush cutter, combination pliers, multitool, or garden clipper (scissors as a last resort)
- [ ] Ziplock bag
- [ ] Paper towels
- [ ] Permanent marker
- [ ] Ruler, mm graduations
- [ ] Thermometer, −10 °C to 60 °C
- [ ] Stopwatch (a phone is fine)
- [ ] Tall pot or container for a water bath
- [ ] Kettle or stove for hot water; ice

# Safety

\safety{
Wear goggles while cutting the pen tip; the brass sleeve can split and eject small fragments. The warmest water bath is only about 40 °C, but handle hot water from the kettle with care and add it to the bath slowly. Spilled glycerin and corn syrup are slippery on hard floors; wipe spills at once. Glycerin and corn syrup are food-grade, and dish soap is a household product; none is hazardous to skin.
}

# Preparation

**0.1** This is the only tricky step in this lab. We will be cutting the very tip of a BIC pen off to extract the ball in the tip of the pen. It's possible you will find this step annoying, but after a lot of experimentation this is the easiest and most repeatable way to get the small ball needed for this lab. If you have a wire cutter, diagonal cutter, flush cutter, combination pliers, multitool, garden clipper, or similar, then this will be quicker and less tedious. If you have nothing else, use scissors, but there is some risk of damaging the edge of your scissors.

Use a medium point BIC Round Stic or BIC Cristal. Hold the body of the pen, keeping your fingers away from the tip where you will cut the pen. Cut the pen at the very tip right behind the ball. The tip will snap off, so you may want to cut inside of a ziplock bag to contain the fragments. Cutting inside of a ziplock ensures you don't lose the ball. If you made the cut perfectly the ball will have fallen out of the brass pen tip. If you cut slightly too far from the tip the brass may stay attached to the pen tip. If the brass is still attached you can either try to break it off, which is tedious, or grab a new pen, which costs 20 cents. Wipe the ball and park it on the magnet. The ball is tungsten carbide, diameter **1.00 mm** (manufacturing tolerance is generally within 0.02 mm), density **15.6 g/cm³**.

**0.2** With the permanent marker, draw a horizontal line around the outside of the cylinder 15 mm below the 100 mL line. This is the upper mark. Using the ruler, draw a second line exactly **50 mm** below the first. This is the lower mark.

**0.3** Stand the cylinder on a level surface.

\photo[id=setup-photo]{Photograph the marked cylinder with the ruler beside it.}

# Part 1 — Four liquids at room temperature

**1.1** Fill the cylinder with water to the 100 mL line.

**1.2** Place the thermometer in the liquid and record **T** to 0.1 °C once the reading has stopped changing. Remove the thermometer. Viscosity changes by several percent for each degree, so a temperature error of even 1 °C badly hurts the accuracy of every result in this lab; measure the temperature in the liquid itself, immediately before each run.

**1.3** Drop the ball into the liquid from just above the surface, aiming for the center of the cylinder. Start the stopwatch as the ball passes the upper mark and stop it as the ball passes the lower mark, sighting each mark at eye level. If the ball drifts visibly toward the side of the cylinder, discard the run. Record **t** to 0.1 s. If a fall is too fast to time, record **t** as "too fast to time".

**1.4** Retrieve the ball: hold the magnet against the outside of the cylinder at the level of the ball and slide it up the wall to the surface, where the ball can be lifted off with a fingertip. Wipe the ball and repeat step 1.3 for a second run.

**1.5** Empty the cylinder, rinse it with warm water, and dry it. Repeat steps 1.1 to 1.4 with dish soap, then corn syrup, then glycerin. Pour the thicker liquids slowly down the inside wall and wait until no bubbles are rising past the marks before dropping the ball. Leave the glycerin in the cylinder.

# Part 2 — Glycerin at five temperatures

The room-temperature glycerin runs from Part 1 are the first of the five temperatures. The glycerin stays in the cylinder for all of Part 2. Each bath below is a pot of water deep enough to reach the 100 mL line. The bath can be a few degrees beyond the target; leave the thermometer in the glycerin, and take the runs as soon as it reads inside the target range, removing the thermometer just before each drop. There is no need to wait for the temperature to settle.

**2.1** Stand the cylinder in an ice-water bath and leave it, with the thermometer in the glycerin, until the glycerin reaches **3 to 8 °C**. Record $T_\mathrm{5}$ and carry out steps 1.3 and 1.4 for two runs, recording $t_\mathrm{5}$.

**2.2** Replace the bath with cool tap water and leave the cylinder in it until the glycerin reaches **11 to 15 °C**. Record $T_\mathrm{13}$ and carry out steps 1.3 and 1.4 for two runs, recording $t_\mathrm{13}$.

**2.3** Replace the bath with warm water and leave the cylinder in it until the glycerin reaches **26 to 30 °C**. Record $T_\mathrm{28}$ and carry out steps 1.3 and 1.4 for two runs, recording $t_\mathrm{28}$.

**2.4** Add hot water to the bath and leave the cylinder in it until the glycerin reaches **33 to 37 °C**. Record $T_\mathrm{35}$ and carry out steps 1.3 and 1.4 for two runs, recording $t_\mathrm{35}$. The fall takes only a few seconds; be ready on the stopwatch before releasing the ball.

**2.5** Return the glycerin to its bottle, park the ball on the magnet, and wash everything with warm water.

From each fall time and the 50 mm mark separation, obtain the terminal velocity of the ball, and use Stokes' law with the ball density and the liquid density to obtain its viscosity. Compare each glycerin result with the accepted value at that temperature. For glycerin, plot $\ln \eta$ against $1/T$ in kelvin, determine the activation energy of viscous flow from the slope, and compare it with the accepted value for glycerin, about $\pu{68 kJ/mol}$, and with the energy of a hydrogen bond, about $\pu{20 kJ/mol}$.

## Accepted viscosity of pure glycerol

\figure[caption="Read the accepted viscosity at your measured temperature from the curve. Dots are the reference measurements of Segur and Oberstar (1951); the curve is the Cheng (2008) fit to them."]{labs/l-1789837730423/1789919429753-cxcsa-glycerol-viscosity.png}

\info[label="Note on supercooled glycerin"]{
Pure glycerol melts at 17.8 °C, so the two coldest runs are below its freezing point. Glycerol almost never crystallizes on its own; it remains a supercooled liquid whose viscosity keeps rising smoothly as it cools, and the part of the curve below 17.8 °C refers to this supercooled liquid. If a bottle ever did freeze it would be an obvious translucent solid.
}

\info[label="Note on the cylinder wall"]{
Stokes' law assumes the ball is falling through an unbounded liquid. In a cylinder this narrow the wall slows the ball by roughly 10%, so every viscosity comes out about that much high. The effect is the same at every temperature, so it does not affect the activation energy.
}

\notes[id=analysis-notes]{Analysis notes}

# Data

Constants: mark separation 50 mm; ball diameter 1.00 mm; ball density 15.6 g/cm³.

\title{Lab 1 — Hess's Law}
\summary{Decompose sodium bicarbonate in a pan, measure two related reactions in a foam-cup calorimeter, and use Hess's law to find the enthalpy of the decomposition.}
\tags{Hess's law, thermochemistry, calorimetry, enthalpy}
\minutes{60}

In this lab you will find the enthalpy change (ΔH) of a reaction you cannot measure directly: baking soda breaking down when it is heated. You will run that reaction in a pan to see what it produces, and then run two different reactions in a foam-cup calorimeter that you *can* measure. Hess's law lets you combine the results of those two measured reactions to calculate ΔH of the one you couldn't measure.

Target reaction (cannot be measured directly):

$$\ce{2 NaHCO3(s) -> Na2CO3(s) + H2O(g) + CO2(g)} \qquad \Delta H = ?$$

| | Reaction | How ΔH is obtained |
|---|---|---|
| A | $\ce{NaHCO3(s) + H+(aq) -> Na+(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)}$ | Measured (Cup A) |
| B | $\ce{Na2CO3(s) + 2 H+(aq) -> 2 Na+(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)}$ | Measured (Cup B) |
| C | $\ce{H2O(l) -> H2O(g)}$ | Given: $\pu{+44.0 kJ/mol}$ |

\info{
Reactions A and B produce liquid water at room temperature; reaction C converts it to the water vapor that actually leaves the pan.
}

Before beginning, use Hess's law to determine how reactions A, B, and C combine to give the target reaction. Every species other than those in the target must cancel. Write the combination and the resulting expression for $\Delta H_{\text{target}}$ in terms of $\Delta H_A$, $\Delta H_B$, and $\Delta H_C$.

\answer[id=hess-derivation, lines=6]{Combination of A, B, and C that yields the target reaction, and the expression for $\Delta H_{\text{target}}$.}

# Materials

**Chemicals**

- [ ] Sodium bicarbonate (baking soda), approximately 6 g
- [ ] Citric acid powder, 12 g
- [ ] Distilled water, 60 mL

**Equipment**

- [ ] Two foam cups, nested
- [ ] Thermometer reading to 0.1 °C
- [ ] Scale reading to 0.01 g (0.1 g acceptable with reduced precision)
- [ ] Small dry skillet or saucepan and a stove (a foil tray may be used in place of the skillet; see Part 1)
- [ ] A drinking glass chilled in the refrigerator or freezer
- [ ] Beaker for the acid solution, metal spoon, match or lighter, graduated cylinder, safety goggles

# Safety

\safety{
Wear safety goggles throughout. The pan in Part 1 reaches approximately 200 °C: handle it only by the handle, keep the exterior dry, and allow it to cool before weighing. Citric acid solution is a mild irritant; rinse any skin contact with water, and rinse eye contact for 15 minutes. The reactions in Part 2 release $\ce{CO2}$ gas. No materials in this experiment are flammable.
}

# Preparation

**0.1**  Weigh **12 g** of citric acid powder and add it to **60 mL** of distilled water in a beaker. Stir until fully dissolved. Dissolving citric acid cools the water, so prepare this solution first and let it stand until it returns to room temperature (about 15 minutes) before Part 2. Label it **1 M citric acid**.

\notes[id=notes-prep]{Notes on preparation}

# Part 1 — Thermal decomposition of sodium bicarbonate

**1.1**  Weigh **4.00 g** of sodium bicarbonate to 0.01 g and record as $m_{\text{start}}$: \input[id=m-start, unit=g]. Weigh the empty, dry pan and record as $m_{\text{pan}}$: \input[id=m-pan, unit=g]. Transfer the sample to the pan and spread it into a thin layer.

**1.2**  Heat the pan on medium. Water vapor and $\ce{CO2}$ are released as the solid decomposes.

**1.3**  Stir occasionally. After approximately 5 minutes, when no further vapor is released, remove the pan from the heat, allow it to cool for 5 minutes, and weigh the pan with residue. Reheat for 2 minutes, cool, and weigh again. Repeat until two consecutive weighings agree within 0.02 g. Record the final value as $m_{\text{pan+residue}}$: \input[id=m-pan-residue, unit=g]

**1.4**  Calculate the residue mass. For complete conversion of $\ce{NaHCO3}$ ($\pu{84.01 g/mol}$) to $\ce{Na2CO3}$ ($\pu{105.99 g/mol}$), the expected residue mass is $m_{\text{start}} \times 105.99 / (2 \times 84.01) = 0.631 \times m_{\text{start}}$, approximately 2.52 g. Record the ratio of measured to expected residue mass: \input[id=residue-ratio]. Retain the residue for Part 2, Cup B.

\tip[label=Note on step 1.1]{
A sheet of aluminum foil folded into a shallow tray with raised edges can be used instead of a skillet. Weigh the empty tray as $m_{\text{pan}}$ and set it directly on the burner. Handle it with tongs; it heats and cools quickly. Because the foil is light, weighing the residue is easier than with a heavy pan.
}

\tip[label=Note on step 1.2]{
The products can be confirmed during heating. Holding a chilled glass inverted about 10 cm above the pan produces condensation from the water vapor, and a lit match lowered to just above the solid is extinguished by the $\ce{CO2}$ accumulating in the pan.
}

\notes[id=notes-part1]{Notes on Part 1}

\photo[id=residue-photo]{Photograph the pan with the residue after the final weighing.}

# Part 2 — Calorimetry

### Calorimeter setup

**2.1**  Nest two foam cups and weigh them. Add approximately **25 mL** of the citric acid solution to the inner cup and weigh again. Record the mass of solution as $m_{\text{acid}}$ to 0.01 g.

**2.2**  Insert the thermometer so the bulb is in the liquid but not touching the bottom, and wait 1 minute. Record the steady temperature as $T_{\text{initial}}$.

### Cup A — sodium bicarbonate

**2.3**  Weigh **2.00 g** of fresh sodium bicarbonate (not the residue) to 0.01 g and record as $m_A$: \input[id=m-a, unit=g]

**2.4**  Start a timer. Add the solid in small portions over approximately 1 minute to control foaming. Transfer the entire sample.

**2.5**  Swirl gently and continuously, reading the thermometer every 15 s. The temperature decreases. Record the lowest temperature reached as $T_{\text{min},A}$: \input[id=t-min-a, unit=°C]. Continue reading for 1 minute past the minimum to confirm it.

### Cup B — decomposition residue from Part 1

**2.6**  Rinse and dry the inner cup. Repeat steps 2.1–2.2 with fresh acid solution and record the new $m_{\text{acid}}$ and $T_{\text{initial}}$.

**2.7**  Weigh **1.50 g** of the Part 1 residue to 0.01 g and record the actual mass as $m_B$: \input[id=m-b, unit=g]

**2.8**  Add the solid in small portions over approximately 1 minute, swirling continuously. The temperature increases. Record the highest temperature reached as $T_{\text{max},B}$: \input[id=t-max-b, unit=°C]

\notes[id=notes-part2]{Notes on Part 2}

Determine $\Delta H_A$ and $\Delta H_B$ in kJ/mol from the calorimetry data, then apply the expression for $\Delta H_{\text{target}}$ you derived at the start of the lab. Compare the result to the accepted value of $\pu{+135.6 kJ}$ per 2 mol $\ce{NaHCO3}$ and compute the percent error. As a final calculation, determine the energy in joules required to fully decompose one teaspoon (approximately 4.6 g) of sodium bicarbonate.

\answer[id=calc-dh, lines=8]{Show your calculation of $\Delta H_A$, $\Delta H_B$, and $\Delta H_{\text{target}}$.}

\answer[id=calc-error, lines=3]{Percent error compared to $\pu{+135.6 kJ}$.}

\answer[id=calc-teaspoon, lines=3]{Energy required to decompose one teaspoon (4.6 g) of sodium bicarbonate.}
